# Nxeon — VPS hosting platform

Hostinger-style VPS hosting platform running on this Proxmox VE 9 dedicated server (OVH KS-GAME, i7-7700K, 64GB RAM, 2×450GB NVMe ZFS mirror + 4TB HDD backup pool).

## Architecture

- **Web panel**: Next.js 15 (App Router, server actions) + Tailwind v4, served by `nxeon-web.service` on port 3000, behind nginx on port 80. Public IP: 51.79.162.96.
- **Worker**: `worker/index.ts` run by `nxeon-worker.service` (as root — it manages iptables). Polls the `Job` table every 3s and executes provisioning/lifecycle jobs against the Proxmox API.
- **DB**: PostgreSQL 17, database `nxeon`, Prisma ORM ([prisma/schema.prisma](prisma/schema.prisma)). Use `npm run db:push` after schema changes.
- **Proxmox**: API token auth (`nxeon@pve!platform`, creds in `.env`). Templates: VMID 9000 (Ubuntu 24.04), 9001 (Debian 13), cloud-init based, cloned onto ZFS storage `vmdata`.
- **Networking**: VMs attach to NAT bridge `vmbr1` (10.20.0.0/24, gateway .1). IPs allocated from 10.20.0.100–250 ([lib/ipam.ts](lib/ipam.ts)). SSH exposed via DNAT port forwards 20000–29999 in iptables chain `NXEON_FWD`, rebuilt from DB by [worker/network.ts](worker/network.ts) — never edit that chain by hand.
- **Cloud-init**: vendor snippet at `/tank/backup/snippets/nxeon-vendor.yaml` (installs qemu-guest-agent, enables root password SSH).

## Portals & design system

**As of 2026-09-14, the customer portal is the "Nexion" redesign** — previously developed in isolation on a separate box (node-2, `/opt/nxeon-v2`, branch `design/v2`) and merged into `main` once it was fully audited and verified. Read this section before touching any shared styling — it is the difference between an edit that stays contained and one that silently reaches marketing, login, or admin.

- **Two portals, two shells, deliberately unmerged:**
  - `app/admin/**` (admin ops portal) still renders through `components/portal/Shell.tsx` — the ORIGINAL, pre-redesign chrome. Marketing (`app/(marketing)/**`), `/login`, `/register` and admin must stay pixel-identical to how they looked before the redesign. Never edit these expecting Nexion's visual language to apply, and never move Nexion-only styling into a place they can see it.
  - `app/dashboard/**` (customer portal) renders through `components/nx/Shell.tsx` — the Nexion redesign. This is where the new design system, its components (`components/nx/*`), and its color/animation language live.
  - **A component added to one shell must be added to the other if it's meant to exist on both.** This has silently broken things before: `ComposeProvider`, `TerminalDockProvider`, `MatrixProvider` were each added to `components/portal/Shell.tsx` first and forgotten on `components/nx/Shell.tsx`, taking a whole feature down invisibly (the crash only appeared on a route a smoke test didn't walk).

- **The scoping trick that keeps the two visually separate — `app/globals.css`, `:root:has(.nx-shell-root)`:**
  Nexion's own colors/tokens and its overrides of shared component classes (`.card`, `.btn-primary`, `.input`, etc.) are NOT bare rules — they're wrapped in `:root:has(.nx-shell-root) { ... }`, a selector that only matches when a `.nx-shell-root` element (rendered only by `components/nx/Shell.tsx`) exists anywhere on the page. That's the entire mechanism keeping marketing/login/admin rendering their original, pre-redesign styles: **do not write a new bare rule for a class both portals share** (e.g. a bare `.card { ... }` outside this scope) — it will apply everywhere, including where it was never meant to.
  - Light mode has its own nested scope for the same reason: `:root:has(.nx-shell-root)[data-theme="light"]`, NOT a bare `html[data-theme="light"]`. The bare form loses a CSS specificity fight to the dark `:has()` block regardless of which theme is active — this was a real, session-spanning bug (several "light mode doesn't work on page X" reports all had this one root cause) before it was scoped correctly.
  - `.nx-dark-island` is a third scope, deliberately staying dark inside the Nexion portal even when light mode is active (site headers, page hero banners) — it re-declares the relevant tokens back to dark values inside `html[data-theme="light"] .nx-dark-island { ... }`. Add a new always-dark token here too if you introduce one (see `--color-neon-bug` for the pattern: declared in the base `@theme` block, overridden lighter in the light-mode scope, re-declared back to its bright value inside `.nx-dark-island`).

- **CSS/JS landmines hit (and fixed) building this — avoid repeating them:**
  - **`@keyframes` and `@property` are not valid nested inside a plain style rule** — only inside `@layer`/`@media`/other at-rules. Nesting one inside `:root:has(...) { }` (or any class selector) silently drops it at build time — no error, the animation just never plays, forever, with every other signal (computed `animation-name`, `animation-play-state: running`) looking correct. This broke ~34 animations at once (a levitating icon, the page preloader, several status dots) when a broad `:has()` refactor accidentally wrapped them. If an animation looks "stuck on frame one," check whether its `@keyframes` block ended up nested inside a style rule.
  - **`backdrop-filter` on an ancestor creates a new containing block for `position: fixed` descendants.** A `.card` with `backdrop-blur-md` breaks any non-portaled modal/overlay nested inside it (it pins to the card instead of the viewport). Fix: cancel the inherited `backdrop-filter` on the offending class, or `createPortal` the fixed element to `document.body`.
  - **A positioned `fixed; z-0` decorative background (an aurora/globe effect) paints above ordinary static content** unless the real content wrapper gets `relative z-[1]`.
  - **Hydration-mismatch anti-pattern**: `useState(() => { if (typeof window === "undefined") return X; ...read window/URL...; return Y; })` — the server always takes the `X` branch, the client's first render always takes `Y`, guaranteed mismatch. Read the value server-side (a Server Component's `searchParams` prop) and pass it down as a real prop instead.
  - Percentage-based `transform: translateY(%)` inside a flex item whose container has no defined width/height resolves against 0 and silently does nothing — give the container a real dimension (e.g. `inset-0` instead of `inset-y-0 right-0` alone) before debugging the animation itself.
  - `git commit -m` with backticks in the message breaks — write the message to a file and use `git commit -F`.
  - Bash `cwd` does not persist between tool calls in an agent session — always `cd /opt/nxeon && ...` in the same command.

- Design system tokens/classes live in `app/globals.css` + `components/ui/primitives.tsx` (shared/production) and `components/nx/*` (Nexion-only). Charts are dependency-free SVG (`components/ui/charts.tsx`) — do not add a charting library.
- Admin impersonation: `impersonateUser()` sets a signed cookie; `currentUser()` returns the target, `realUser()` the actual admin; banner + exit handled in Shell. Admin pages call `realUser`/`requireAdmin` and refuse to render while impersonating.
- Metrics come from Proxmox RRD via `/api/metrics` (node for admins, per-server for owners). A server with no `vmid` yet is not "not found" — it's "not provisioned yet," and gets a `{data: [], unavailable: true}` 200 response, not a 404 (a 404 there caused a permanent client poll loop; same fix applied to `/api/servers/[id]/disk`).

## Working on this codebase — one tree, any session

`/opt/nxeon` (this directory, branch `main`) is the single source of truth. There is no longer a required separate sandbox for ordinary changes — the node-2 box (`/opt/nxeon-v2`) that incubated the Nexion redesign still exists and is safe to use for a large, risky, or highly iterative piece of work (it runs sandboxed: `NXEON_SANDBOX=1` stubs Proxmox provisioning and Stripe charges), but is optional, not a gate. Any session — this one or another — can edit `main` directly and ship through the pipeline below.

1. Edit, then `npx tsc --noEmit` before building anything.
2. `npm run build` locally only to catch build errors before pushing — do not restart production services from an ad hoc build in this directory (see Commands below); this is validation, not deployment.
3. Commit (small, real commits — the GitHub post-commit hook auto-pushes `origin`).
4. `scripts/deploy-staging.sh <ref>` — builds, migrates, and restarts staging (`:8080`) from that ref. **Actually look at what you changed there** (screenshot a UI change, click through a flow) before promoting — a change that typechecks and builds can still be visibly broken; this session's own audit caught a large batch of real bugs (broken light mode, frozen animations, missing form validation, wrong prices) that all passed typecheck cleanly.
5. `scripts/promote-production.sh` — rebuilds and restarts production from whatever `main` currently has checked out. It refuses to run if staging isn't healthy first.

If two sessions are likely to be editing at once, coordinate the ordinary way: pull before starting, small commits, push often (the auto-push hook does this for you on commit).

## Integrations (activate via /opt/nxeon/.env)

- **Stripe**: `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` + `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` → wallet top-ups switch from demo gateway to Checkout (`/api/stripe/checkout`, webhook `/api/stripe/webhook`, event `checkout.session.completed`, idempotent by session id). Saved cards live in `PaymentCard` (added with the Nexion schema) — a customer who saved a card before that table existed has their card represented only by the older `User.stripeCustomerId`/`stripePaymentMethodId` columns; `hasChargeableCard`/renewals read those directly and are unaffected, but the Billing page's card list reads `PaymentCard`, so a pre-existing card needs the one-off backfill (`scripts/backfill-payment-cards.ts`) to show up there. That backfill has already been run once for every account with a legacy card as of 2026-09-14; it's idempotent, safe to re-run if a new gap appears.
- **Namecheap** (`lib/namecheap.ts`): `NAMECHEAP_API_USER/KEY/USERNAME/CLIENT_IP` (+`NAMECHEAP_SANDBOX=1` for testing) → domain search/register/renew/DNS management. TLD retail prices in `TLD_PRICES`.
- **GitHub**: remote `origin` = `git@github.com:santino1233/nxeon.git` via deploy key `/root/.ssh/nxeon_deploy`. Every commit auto-pushes via `.git/hooks/post-commit`. `.env`/credentials are gitignored — never commit secrets.

## Conventions

- All state changes to VMs go through `Job` rows — the web app never calls Proxmox mutation endpoints directly (read-only status calls are OK).
- One in-flight job per server (enforced in `serverAction`).
- Admin-only actions live in [lib/actions.ts](lib/actions.ts) and must call `requireAdmin()`.
- Free VPSes: `Server.isFree = true`, no billing, `expiresAt = null`.
- Wallet amounts are integer cents.
- Never fabricate: no invented stats, ratings, reviews, player counts, or ETAs. If a number can't be read from the database or a real upstream, the field stays empty and the UI says why — this tree has had hash-derived star ratings and fake reviews removed once already.
- Minecraft subdomains (`*.play.nxeon.cloud`) are shared across two tables — `FreeMinecraftServer.subdomain` and `Server.subdomain` — because both products resolve under the same DNS zone. Always check availability through `lib/game-subdomain.ts`'s `isSubdomainAvailable()` (queries both) rather than checking either table alone, or a free and a paid server can claim the same name.

## Documentation — keep it current (required)

- **Every change, fix, or addition MUST update `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` in the same commit.** Add a dated bullet to §15 (Change history) and edit any section the change affects (data model, subsystems, feature catalog, integrations, roadmap, etc.). A commit that changes behaviour without touching the docs is incomplete.
- Keep `ROADMAP.md` in sync too: check off / move the item you completed.
- `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` is the single source of truth. The public mirror at `https://revsports.ca/docs` is regenerated from it with `node scripts/publish-docs.mjs` (zero-dep markdown→styled-HTML renderer → `/var/www/nxeon-docs/index.html`) — run that after editing the doc so the hosted page matches. The `/docs` nginx location lives in `scripts/configure-domains.sh` so it survives vhost regeneration.
- The claude.ai artifact webpage (`https://claude.ai/code/artifact/9b0c97f5-4c34-4f89-bee9-b5a80eb23892`) can only be updated from an interactive Claude Code session (headless/cron runs can't reach it) — that refresh is best-effort, the repo doc + `/docs` page are authoritative.

## Commands

- Typecheck: `npx tsc --noEmit` (always, before a build)
- Build: `npm run build` (must pass before restarting services)
- Deploy after changes: `npm run build && systemctl restart nxeon-web nxeon-worker` — or, preferably, go through `scripts/deploy-staging.sh` → verify → `scripts/promote-production.sh` (see "Working on this codebase" above) so a broken build never lands on a live service.
- Worker logs: `journalctl -u nxeon-worker -f`
- E2E test: `npx tsx scripts/e2e-test.ts` (orders a real VM; delete it afterwards via a DELETE job)
- Admin credentials: `/root/nxeon-credentials.txt`

## Domains & TLS

- **Single source of truth**: `/etc/nxeon/domains.env` (BASE_DOMAIN, ADMIN_HOST, STAGING_HOST, CERTBOT_EMAIL). The domain is a placeholder (`revsports.ca`) until the real one is bought. **Never hardcode the domain anywhere in app code** — the app uses `APP_URL` / `NXEON_ADMIN_HOST` from `.env`, and nginx vhosts are generated.
- **To migrate to a new domain**: edit `/etc/nxeon/domains.env`, point DNS (A records for apex, www, admin host, staging host) at the server, then run `scripts/configure-domains.sh`. It regenerates nginx vhosts, obtains Let's Encrypt certs, updates APP_URL in both `.env`s, and restarts web. That's the whole migration.
- **Routing**: customer portal on `https://BASE_DOMAIN` (admin path returns 404 here — hidden); admin ops portal on `https://ADMIN_HOST` (secret subdomain, root 302→/admin); staging on `https://STAGING_HOST`. HTTP→HTTPS 301. Real LE cert (auto-renews via certbot timer); self-signed fallback for bare-IP. A raw `http://51.79.162.96:8080` fallback listener also exists for staging (no TLS, no forwarded headers) — it's a debug path only, not how a real customer or any Server Action's origin check expects to be reached; testing against it directly produces false failures (CSP/origin-check errors) that don't reproduce on the real `STAGING_HOST`.
- Secure cookies are on (`COOKIE_SECURE=1`) now that real HTTPS exists. Stripe webhook is live at `https://BASE_DOMAIN/api/stripe/webhook`.

## Environments

- **Production**: `/opt/nxeon`, DB `nxeon`, services `nxeon-web` (port 3000) + `nxeon-worker`, nginx port 80, VPS pools IP 10.20.0.100–250 / SSH ports 20000–29999, NAT chain `NXEON_FWD`. Public: http://51.79.162.96
- **Staging**: `/opt/nxeon-staging`, DB `nxeon_staging`, services `nxeon-staging-web` (port 3001) + `nxeon-staging-worker`, nginx port 8080, ISOLATED VPS pools IP 10.20.0.50–99 / SSH ports 30000–30999, NAT chain `NXEON_FWD_STG`, VM tag `nxeon-staging`. Public: http://51.79.162.96:8080 (see the TLS note above — prefer `STAGING_HOST` over the bare port for anything that exercises real form submissions). Admin creds: `/root/nxeon-staging-credentials.txt`.
- **node-2 sandbox** (optional, not required): `nxeon-fsn1` (178.63.94.114), tree at `/opt/nxeon-v2`, its own DB (`nxeon_v2`), `NXEON_SANDBOX=1` (stubs Proxmox provisioning + Stripe charges only — everything else is real code against a real, separate DB). Useful for large or highly experimental work in isolation; not part of the normal edit→stage→promote path above. Root SSH from node-2 to this box exists (`scripts/node1.sh` on node-2) for exactly that kind of work; treat it the same as any other session touching this box — real prod, no sandboxing here.
- Instance differences are driven entirely by `.env` (NXEON_ENV, NXEON_COOKIE_NAME, NXEON_NAT_CHAIN, NXEON_TAG, NXEON_IP_START/END, NXEON_SSH_PORT_START/END, NXEON_CRED_FILE, PORT, APP_URL) — the code is identical.
- **Deploy flow**: push to GitHub → `scripts/deploy-staging.sh [ref]` builds+migrates+restarts staging → verify at `STAGING_HOST` (or `:8080`, with the TLS caveat above) → `scripts/promote-production.sh` rebuilds+restarts production. Test changes on staging before promoting — always.

## Safety rules

- NEVER touch VMIDs 9000–9999 (templates) except to add new templates.
- Staging and production share the Proxmox node but never overlap: staging only ever allocates IPs .50–.99 and ports 30000–30999. Never point staging pools at production ranges.
- Test risky/provisioning changes on staging (`scripts/deploy-staging.sh`) before promoting to production.
- Never `qm destroy` a VM that has a `Server` row — always go through a DELETE job.
- Never `pkill -f` by pattern on this box — kill by port PID or systemd unit instead (a pattern match has restarted live production before).
- Do not commit `.env`. Do not print the Proxmox token into logs or docs.
- Always `git commit` working states; never leave the tree broken — services restart from this directory.

 * A customer-defined automatic action on a GAME server — MVP: a daily restart at
 * a fixed UTC time. The worker sweep (worker/game-control.ts gameScheduleSweep)
 * enqueues a GAME_POWER restart when `nextRunAt` falls due, optionally announcing
 * the restart to connected players over RCON first.
 * `nextRunAt` is the single source of truth the sweep selects on; it is (re)computed
 * from `hour`/`minute` whenever the row is created, edited, or fires. All times are
 * UTC in the MVP (the UI states this) — no per-customer timezone yet.
 */
model GameSchedule {
  id              String    @id @default(cuid())
  serverId        String
  server          Server    @relation(fields: [serverId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
  kind            String    @default("restart")
  command         String?
  hour            Int // 0..23 (UTC) — used for daily (non-interval) schedules
  minute          Int // 0..59
  intervalMinutes Int?
  enabled         Boolean   @default(true)
  announce        Boolean   @default(true)
  lastRunAt       DateTime?
  nextRunAt       DateTime?
  createdAt       DateTime  @default(now())
  updatedAt       DateTime  @updatedAt

  @@index([enabled, nextRunAt])
  @@index([serverId])
}

model PortForward {
  id         String @id @default(cuid())
  serverId   String
  server     Server @relation(fields: [serverId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
  publicPort Int    @unique
  guestPort  Int
  protocol   String @default("tcp")
}

enum FirewallDirection {
  INBOUND
}

enum FirewallAction {
  ALLOW
  DENY
}

enum FirewallProtocol {
  TCP
  UDP
  ICMP
  ALL
}

model FirewallRule {
  id         String            @id @default(cuid())
  serverId   String
  server     Server            @relation(fields: [serverId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
  direction  FirewallDirection @default(INBOUND)
  action     FirewallAction
  protocol   FirewallProtocol
  portFrom   Int?
  portTo     Int?
  sourceCidr String?           @default("0.0.0.0/0")
  comment    String?
  enabled    Boolean           @default(true)
  position   Int               @default(0)
  createdAt  DateTime          @default(now())

  @@index([serverId])
}

content.thinking:
This involves significant money movement, so I want to keep fulfilment honest and simple: I'll write pure helper functions for snapshotting, pricing, and transitions in one file, and a separate fulfilment module that handles the actual DB writes—creating the Plan/GamePlan rows, Server row, invoice, and job. For game offers specifically, I need to work out the template ID, variant, and default game config.

For game offers, staff pick a family and variant, then at fulfilment time I pull the schema's order defaults and validate against them—customers can adjust settings after deploy, and subdomain stays null. On placement, I'll respect a pinned node if staff set one (checking it's enabled), otherwise fall back to region-based placement with capacity checks on RAM and disk. If capacity fails after payment, the money stays safely in the wallet and the offer stays ACCEPTED with a fulfilment error flagged for admin review rather than silently failing. I'm also mapping out the accept flow starting with a server action that authenticates and validates the offer before checkout.

Now I'm working through the total calculation, including whether tax should apply to offers the same way it does for regular orders—leaning toward yes for consistency, pulling the rate from the user's billing country, though I need to check if tax is on by default. For fulfilment, I'm designing an idempotent transaction: atomically transition the offer status, then debit the wallet and create the plan, server, invoice, and job in one go, treating a failed status transition as a signal that the offer was already claimed.

This status-CAS approach relies on Postgres's row-level locking under READ COMMITTED—a concurrent updater blocks until the first transaction commits, then re-evaluates and finds nothing to update, which naturally prevents double-fulfilment. For partial wallet coverage, I'm planning a Stripe Checkout session for just the remainder, marking the offer ACCEPTED and storing the session ID, then on payment confirmation crediting the wallet and fulfilling using the stored charge amount—while thinking through the edge case where staff cancels the offer while checkout is still open, which would leave money sitting in the wallet needing admin attention.

I should also expire the Stripe session on cancellation as a best-effort cleanup, and handle the grace period where a payment completes just after expiry but the session was created while still valid. There's also a wallet-balance race if the customer spends elsewhere between checkout creation and payment confirmation—fulfilment would fail on insufficient balance, leaving the offer ACCEPTED with an error state the customer can retry once covered.

For double-clicking accept and creating duplicate checkout sessions, I want to reuse an existing open session if one was created recently, returning its client secret instead of creating a new one; if both somehow get paid, the second fulfilment just no-ops since the offer is already PAID, with the money safely credited to wallet rather than lost. I also need to wire the offer branch into the confirm route's fulfilment runner with a redirect back to the offer page, add the offer key to the session classifier so it's excluded from top-up invoicing, and handle best-effort card saving from the payment session.

With setup_future_usage set to off_session and the Stripe customer ensured, if the wallet fully covers the charge no card gets saved, so autoRenew will just depend on whatever card already exists — that seems fine. I want to double check the stripe-cards comments for the 2026-10-01 API version before moving on.

I'm thinking through how offers should handle anonymous visitors without a userId—accepting an offer requires a customer account, so I need to decide whether to bind the offer to the conversation and email instead, letting the customer "claim" it later by signing in with a matching verified email, or simply require the conversation to already be linked to an account.

Binding an offer by an unverified chat-supplied email is risky since an anonymous visitor could type someone else's email and have staff accidentally send an offer tied to that person's account, so I'm deciding to require a signed-in conversation (convo.userId) strictly, with staff able to send directly via userId from the admin customer page instead. Now I'm working out the OfferCard component for chat and the API endpoint to fetch offer data—since offers only bind to signed-in users, the viewer resolves from the session cookie for customers, while staff need a separate "real user" check for their view.

I'm now mapping out the broader architecture: Prisma models for Offer, OfferEvent, and OfferTask with their enums; a pure pricing module for specs, snapshots, validation, and transitions; a server module handling offer lifecycle operations like drafting, sending, cancelling, and expiry sweeps; a fulfillment module for payment transactions; server actions split between staff and customer operations; and Stripe/checkout integration pieces for the purchase flow.

I'm also sketching UI pieces -- an API route for fetching offer cards, admin composer and offer list pages with per-customer filtering, a reusable composer form abstracting over conversation vs. user targets, a section on the admin user detail page linking to offers, and customer-facing dashboard pages for viewing and paying offers via Stripe checkout. For expiry, I'm deciding lazy checks at read/accept/fulfil time are sufficient rather than needing a dedicated worker sweep.

enum VmMoveStatus {
  PLANNED // dry-run finished, or a real move queued but not yet started
  RUNNING
  DONE // cutover committed; source VM kept STOPPED until VM_MOVE_CLEANUP
  ROLLED_BACK // a phase before commit failed; source running again, target removed
  FAILED // rollback itself did not fully succeed — needs a human (see `error`)
  CLEANED // source VM destroyed by VM_MOVE_CLEANUP
}

model VmMove {
  id              String       @id @default(cuid())
  serverId        String

  plan            Json?
  checkpoints     Json?
  log             Json?
  error           String?
  addressChanged  Boolean      @default(false)
  keepSourceUntil DateTime?
  sourceCleanedAt DateTime?
  startedAt       DateTime?
  finishedAt      DateTime?
  createdAt       DateTime     @default(now())
  updatedAt       DateTime     @updatedAt

  @@index([serverId])
  @@index([status])
}

content.thinking:
I'm defining the pricing types and draft input structure for offers in a pure, client-safe module, covering kind, terms, and spec fields like CPU and RAM.

I'm making sure the customer-facing view strips out internal notes, catalog data, and margin info, since terms should only expose what the customer needs to see. Then I'm sketching validation rules for offer input—checking title length, CPU/RAM/disk ranges for VPS and GAME kinds, storage tier options, term limits, and ensuring pricing fields like renewal and first-term costs stay within sane bounds.

Next I'm defining helper functions: one to derive a discounted first-term price from a percentage, one to compute total due amounts including setup fees and IP costs, and one to calculate the promotional discount percent by comparing first-term to full renewal pricing. I'm also starting to build a function that assembles the customer-facing offer terms using contextual data like OS and node names.

I also need to decide where hashing lives since it requires Node's crypto module—I'll keep the pricing calculations client-safe and move hashing into a server-side module, with a stable stringify function shared between them. Then I'm sketching validation for parsing offer snapshots and the status transition logic, including an `effectiveStatus` function that marks offers as expired once their expiration time passes, while thinking through edge cases like accepting an already-expired offer.

For the accepted-but-expiring-during-payment case, I'm defining a grace period of two hours to cover the one-hour Stripe checkout window, so an offer only flips to expired if payment completes too late relative to that window. I'm also working out how to generate customer-facing spec lines for invoices—deciding to show the region rather than the internal node name to keep things appropriate for customer display.

I'm now sketching out invoice line generation (description, term label, spec lines, discount, setup fee, IP charge) and a margin calculator that derives cost share and margin percentage from renewal price, RAM allocation, and node costs. For tax, I'm computing the due-now amount at acceptance time based on the customer's tax rate, with renewals handled separately through the billing sweep. Now I'm moving into writing the actual fulfilment function.

The fulfilment flow validates the offer belongs to the requesting user, treats already-paid offers as idempotent successes, checks the offer is still in a payable state (not expired, correct status for wallet vs card), re-parses and hash-verifies the terms, then computes totals including tax before gross amount. I'm working through the pre-transaction resolution steps needed before committing the payment.

pinned, skip the global RAM check and just verify disk capacity on that specific node, since staff pinning is an explicit documented override. Next I'm moving into the transaction logic, starting with the CAS-style updateMany on the offer.

Still defining task rows and offer event...

For insufficient balance, I throw an error the caller catches and marks as fulfilError. After commit, I run audit logging, send the invoice email and customer notification best-effort, and consider whether to accrue partner commissions now versus letting the background sweep handle it later, since offers are custom-negotiated and commission rules are murky here.

For the card payment path, I credit the wallet first, then claim the fulfilled session, then attempt fulfilOffer — if that fails, the money stays safely in the wallet, settlement is marked FAILED, the customer gets notified, and a staff task is created. I'm also handling the edge case where an offer gets cancelled mid-checkout (expiring the stripe session best-effort, but still crediting wallet if payment lands anyway) and where the wallet balance might be insufficient if the customer spent funds elsewhere in the meantime — in that case fulfilError lets them retry via Accept & Pay.

For a hostname conflict during the transaction, I'm just throwing a friendly error and letting the whole transaction roll back, which naturally reverts the status change too since it's in the same tx.

Now I'm sketching the acceptOffer action for customers — checking auth, impersonation, email verification, ownership, lazy expiry, and whether the offer is in a payable state (SENT/VIEWED/ACCEPTED and not expired, with ACCEPTED allowed only if still before expiresAt).

Next I need pre-flight capacity checking mirroring fulfilment logic but without writes, computing totals and tax to get the gross amount, then splitting between wallet and card. If the card portion is zero, I either error out for insufficient balance below Stripe's minimum or fulfil directly via wallet; otherwise I mark the offer ACCEPTED with a CAS guard, and either reuse an existing open checkout session matching the amount or create a new one.

For the checkout metadata, I'm debating whether to store just the offer reference or also snapshot the gross/tax amounts, since tax could shift if the user's billing country changes between acceptance and payment — to stay safe I'll include grossCents and taxCents in metadata so fulfilment can sanity-check against the recomputed values and use the accepted amount the customer actually saw and paid.

Now I'm working through the decline flow (transitioning SENT/VIEWED/ACCEPTED to DECLINED with an event and a chat notification for staff) and the viewed flow (CAS SENT→VIEWED with a timestamp when the customer opens the offer). Then I'm starting on the staff-side server actions, beginning with building the offer composer context that gathers customer info, catalog plans, game families, OS templates, node cost data, and IP pricing.

Since the composer is used in live chat by SUPPORT staff who lack billing access, I'm deciding to gate it behind a billing-area requirement so SUPPORT sees an access message while ADMIN/BILLING/EMPLOYEE can proceed. I'm also outlining the remaining actions: quoting an offer with margin and totals, creating a draft offer, sending it, canceling it, and completing related tasks.

For sending, I'm working out how to snapshot and hash the terms, mark status as SENT, and compute expiresAt from the expiry days—storing a provisional expiry on draft creation and validating it isn't null or past at send time. If there's a conversationId tied to the offer, I also want to post a chat message when the offer is sent.

Still working out the chat message content—something like "Offer #N: title — $X first term, then $Y/mo. Review here: link" with an offer card attached, writing directly to the db similar to the existing chat reply pattern, and best-effort mirroring to Discord. I also need to send an email to the customer linking to the dashboard offer page, using whatever email template shell function already exists.

I'm thinking through the "ALREADY_HANDLED" failure case — if another concurrent caller already won and the status is no longer open but also not PAID (like a concurrent cancellation), that's a legitimate failure to record. The FulfilledSession claim guards against duplicate fulfilment for the same session, but I need to consider the separate scenario where a customer double-pays across two different sessions.

In that duplicate-payment case, the second session's fulfilOffer call returns already=true since the offer was already marked PAID by the first; the money still lands in the wallet silently aside from the generic payment notification, which is acceptable since the balance is visible, but I think it's better to flag it for staff — I'll detect `already=true` in the card branch and create a DUPLICATE_PAYMENT OfferTask with a note, since this path can only be reached by a genuinely different session (the same-session race would already be stopped by the FulfilledSession claim before fulfilOffer is called).

For the accept-offer flow, I'm sketching the logic: blocking impersonators, requiring a verified user and email, rate-limiting attempts, validating the offer belongs to the user and isn't a draft, checking expiry and payment status, extracting trusted terms safely, and attempting to resolve placement before emitting an offer event on failure.

Then I'm computing the amount due and splitting it between wallet balance and card based on the useWallet flag -- if the card portion is zero, it either errors out for insufficient balance or fulfills the offer entirely via wallet. Otherwise it proceeds with the card leg by atomically transitioning the offer's status to ACCEPTED (failing if the row was already in an unexpected state) and recording an acceptance event the first time through.

Now I'm checking whether there's an existing checkout session for this offer that still matches the required card amount and gross total -- if so, I can just retrieve its client_secret and reuse it rather than creating a duplicate, falling back to creating a new session if the client_secret isn't present or the amounts no longer line up; I also want to expire the stale session if it doesn't match so there aren't two live payable sessions at once. If creating a new checkout session fails, I return an error indicating card payments aren't configured and suggest topping up the wallet instead.

I note that acceptedAt matters for the card grace period — if the offer is re-accepted after expiry, canStartPayment should block it, which is correct — and there's a subtlety where the card path's wallet split uses the balance at accept time, so if the balance drops before fulfillment debits the gross amount, the payment could fail even though the card portion was already charged, which needs to be documented.

content.thinking:
All tests pass, and the stripe import connecting lazily to prisma shouldn't be an issue since other tests follow the same pattern. Now I'm setting up the DB test file, seeding users and an os template with slug, name, vmid fields, planning to create custom plans rather than relying on existing ones.

I'm checking that dedicated IP pricing falls back to a default of zero cents when the env var isn't set, which should be fine for the test. The DB test will call lib functions directly like createOfferDraft, sendOffer, fulfilOffer, and fulfilRetrievedCheckoutSession with fake Stripe sessions, since the fake secret key means any real network calls to Stripe will fail but should be caught as best-effort errors — though I need to verify the mailer doesn't hang trying to reach an unconfigured SMTP server. I'm sketching out the test list, starting with create+send verifying frozen terms and hash, then edit behavior.

Next I'm covering: live column edits after send shouldn't affect the frozen snapshot used for viewing and fulfillment; auth checks for getOfferForViewer across different customers, draft visibility, and staff access; viewed-marking; and a concurrency test where three simultaneous fulfilOffer calls against a wallet-funded user should resolve to exactly one successful provisioning with balance hitting zero (not negative), one invoice, and the correct already-fulfilled flags on the other two calls. I also want to verify server fields like grandfathered renewal cents, discount percentages, refundable term cents, expiry date, the PROVISION job, CPU pinning/priority tasks, multi-line invoice amounts, and that a subsequent renewal charge nets to exactly 7580 cents. Then I'm planning a card-payment path test with a second user at zero balance, manually setting the offer to accepted, and calling fulfilRetrievedCheckoutSession concurrently (simulating webhook plus return, then a late return) to check idempotency.

Then I move to several more scenarios: a duplicate second payment session should credit the wallet and spawn a note task without creating a second server; wallet-based fulfillment should be refused for expired offers while card payments accepted just before expiry should still be honored within a grace window (testing with manipulated acceptedAt/expiresAt timestamps); checkout cancelled mid-flow should refuse fulfillment, keep the money in the wallet, and fire a FULFIL_FAILED task without creating a server; tampering with the stored terms JSON should cause fulfillment to be refused; dedicated server offers should only generate an invoice and DEDICATED_BUILD task without provisioning a server or plan; game server offers need a game OsTemplate with proper schema validation and should create a GamePlan plus server with the right gameVariant, including renewal behavior; and pinned-node offers should assign the server to a specific unreachable seeded node, which I'll test last. I'm also noting I need to check what capacitySnapshot does when there are no nodes, possibly reaching out to Proxmox via environment variables.

content.thinking:
I'm checking whether staging has a publishable key too, since a true browser e2e through the embedded Stripe checkout would need Playwright driving the card entry iframe — doable but heavy. I'm weighing alternatives, like creating a real test-mode Checkout Session and completing it through a hosted Playwright flow, since sessions can't be paid directly via the API.

A more realistic plan: call createOfferCheckout with the real test key to confirm Stripe accepts the params, retrieve the session via API to verify metadata and test the reuse logic, then simulate payment by confirming a PaymentIntent with a test card and feeding a paid-looking session object into fulfilRetrievedCheckoutSession to confirm the card gets saved for renewals, before expiring the real session afterward. I'm also still considering just running Playwright against the embedded checkout in the dev server and filling the iframe with the 4242 test card for a genuine full end-to-end run.

Stripe's embedded checkout iframes should be fillable with Playwright's frame locators, so I'll try the browser e2e first and fall back to the API approach if it fails — I'll need to point the confirm route's return_url at localhost and spin up a dev server anyway since I need one for screenshots. Test mode shouldn't trip any real-money safeguards, and since webhooks can't reach localhost, fulfillment will have to happen via the redirect confirm route. The tricky part is setting up the dev server's env: I need throwaway DB, APP_URL, test Stripe keys, auth secret, and cookie settings, but I want to avoid copying the staging env's real Proxmox credentials since the web app shouldn't need to mutate Proxmox directly outside of worker jobs.

Since the worktree has no .env file, I'll just pass the minimal required variables directly on the command line rather than copying staging's full config, so let me check which variable names staging actually uses.

# Part VII — Change history

Everything below this line is **history**, not reference. It is kept because the *reasons* recorded in
these entries are often the only surviving explanation for why a piece of code looks the way it does.
Where an entry contradicts Parts I–VI, **Parts I–VI win** — they were verified against the tree; these
were written at the time.

## How to read the change history

```
 Part VII is ordered oldest → newest in three layers:
   1. "Change history — the first 28 commits"   the compressed early record
   2. dated / titled entries                    one H2 per shipped change
   3. "Session log — 2026-07-26/27"             the most recent waves
 Authoritative alternatives when an entry looks stale:
   git log --date=short --pretty='%h|%ad|%s'
   git blame <file> -L <start>,<end>
```

## Custom offers: staff-built quotes customers accept and pay (2026-10-06, branch `feature/chat-offers`)

**Why.** A custom VPS negotiated in live chat (6 vCPU / 32 GB / 120 GB NVMe on node-6, pinned CPU + CPU priority, first month 50% off, then $75.80/mo) had to be fulfilled by hand: tell the customer to top up, hand-insert `Plan` + `Server` + a `PROVISION` job in SQL, set CPU priority/pinning on the host, debit the wallet, hand-write the invoice. Offers replace that whole flow with one auditable money path.

**Data model (additive only — 3 tables + 2 enums, no column/relation added to any existing model).** `Offer` (spec columns, pricing columns, status, lifecycle timestamps, `terms` JSON snapshot + `termsHash`, result `serverId`/`invoiceId`/`planId`/`gamePlanId`, `fulfilError`, `checkoutSessionId`), `OfferEvent` (append-only audit trail), `OfferTask` (manual follow-ups). FK-less string ids, like `NodeAlert`.

**Money model (`lib/offer-pricing.ts`, pure).** `renewalMonthlyCents` R is stored on the server as `grandfatheredRenewalCents` with `annualDiscountPct = 0`, so `renewalCharge` renews at exactly R x term (asserted against the real function in tests). `firstTermCents` F (<= R x term) is the whole first term; `termPromoPercent` = % off R x term (the proration basis); `refundableTermCents` = F. Terms are **1 or 12 months only** (24/36 carry fixed `VPS_TERMS` discounts renewalCharge would apply on top of R). Setup fee is one-time. Dedicated IP is billed at the platform rate (snapshotted at send) on the first invoice and every renewal, its own line + `Invoice.dedicatedIpCents`. VAT/GST is added at accept time from the customer's billing country (`lib/tax.ts`).

**Lifecycle.** `DRAFT -> SENT -> VIEWED -> ACCEPTED -> PAID`, or `EXPIRED / CANCELLED / DECLINED` (terminal). Sending freezes the terms (snapshot + sha256); fulfilment only ever reads the snapshot and re-checks the hash, so editing the row after send changes nothing the customer accepted. Expiry is applied lazily on read (`effectiveOfferStatus`, persisted by `persistExpiry`) — no cron needed. An ACCEPTED offer (customer opened card checkout before expiry) is still honoured for `OFFER_PAYMENT_GRACE_MS` (2h) after expiry; the wallet path never gets grace.

**Staff side.** `components/admin/chat/OfferComposer.tsx` (`<OfferComposer conversationId onSent/>` for the live-chat desk's "Send offer" button; `<OfferComposerForm target={{userId}|{conversationId}}/>` elsewhere). Pre-fills from a catalog VPS plan / game tier; the server-side preview shows the self-serve price for the same spec (exact catalog match, else `customPlanQuote`/`customGamePlanQuote`, else the smallest catalog plan covering it) and the **margin vs the node's real monthly cost apportioned by RAM** (`Node.monthlyCostCents x ramMB / capacityRamMB`). Admin page `/admin/offers` (billing area; nav: Billing -> Revenue & invoices -> Custom offers): list/filter, per customer (`?userId=`), from a chat (`?conversationId=&new=1`), detail + audit trail (`?offer=`), cancel/send draft, and the **Manual follow-ups** panel. The customer page has a "Custom offer" button. RBAC: every staff action is `requireGrant("billing")` (ADMIN, BILLING, or an EMPLOYEE granted billing) — SUPPORT-only staff see the composer refuse; every create/send/cancel/task-done is in `OfferEvent` and `AuditLog` (`offer.*`, category billing). Sending posts an agent `ChatMessage` with `cardsJson = [{"type":"offer","key":"offer:<id>","offerId":"<id>"}]`, a portal notification, and optionally an email with the link. A chat offer requires the visitor to be **signed in** (the offer must belong to an account); an anonymous thread is refused with a clear message.

## Custom offers: done, committed, not merged or deployed

Staff can now build a priced offer for a VPS, game server or dedicated server. The customer reviews it and pays with **Accept & Pay**. Paying creates the invoice and the server, and queues PROVISION. I tested it end to end in Stripe test mode on a throwaway stack. Typecheck is clean, and the full test suite adds no new failures caused by this code.

**Branch:** `feature/chat-offers`, commit `3bfd710146`, worktree `/tank/nxeon-wt-offers`. 21 files, staged by explicit path, no node_modules in the commit. The post-commit hook only pushes `main`, so this branch has not been pushed.

**One change from your setup instructions:** I did not symlink node_modules. Generating the Prisma client would have written into prod's `/opt/nxeon/node_modules`. Instead the worktree has its own copy (1.2 GB on /tank) and the client was generated there. Prod's client is untouched.

### Data model (additive only)
- **New tables:** `Offer`, `OfferEvent` (audit trail) and `OfferTask` (manual follow-ups), plus enums `OfferKind` (VPS | GAME | DEDICATED) and `OfferStatus` (DRAFT … DECLINED).
- **Nothing existing changes:** no column or relation is added to any existing model. Links to user, server and invoice are plain string ids.
- **Offer contents:**
  - Typed spec fields: vCPU, RAM, disk, storage tier, bandwidth, OS, game family/variant/basis plan, slots, node or region, hostname.
  - Extras as flags: CPU priority, CPU pinning, dedicated IP. Customer notes plus a staff-only internal note.
  - Pricing: first-term price, monthly renewal price, term, setup fee, discount label/percent, USD.
  - Lifecycle timestamps and actors, `checkoutSessionId`, `fulfilError`, and the resulting server/invoice/plan ids.
- **Frozen terms:** sending stores a `terms` JSON snapshot plus its sha256 (`termsHash`). Fulfilment bills only from the snapshot and re-checks the hash, so editing an offer after sending can't change what the customer accepted (tested).

### Money path
1. **Staff compose** (`components/admin/chat/OfferComposer.tsx`, props `{conversationId, onSent}`; the same form takes a `userId` target on `/admin/offers`).
   - It pre-fills from a catalog plan or game tier.
   - It shows the self-serve price for the same spec: exact catalog match, else `customPlanQuote`/`customGamePlanQuote`, else the smallest catalog plan that covers it.
   - It shows margin against the node's real monthly cost, split by RAM. For the real case on node-6: $51.85/mo, 68.4%.
   - Every staff action requires billing access (`requireGrant("billing")`) and is written to the offer's audit trail and `AuditLog`.
2. **Send** posts an agent chat message with `cardsJson = [{"type":"offer","key":"offer:<id>","offerId":"<id>"}]`, adds a portal notification, and optionally emails a link.
3. **Customer views** the card (`components/chat/cards/OfferCard.tsx`, also wired into `ChatWidget` via `type:"offer"`) or `/dashboard/offers/[id]`. Customers see only their own offers that have been sent; anything else is a 404.
4. **Accept & Pay** (`acceptOfferAction`):
   - It is blocked while impersonating and goes through the email-verification gate.
   - It checks image, game config, node and capacity before any money moves.
   - If the wallet covers the amount, the offer is fulfilled immediately.
   - Otherwise it opens Stripe Embedded Checkout (`createOfferCheckout`) with a real Customer and `setup_future_usage: off_session`. An open session with the same amounts is reused; a stale one is expired.
5. **Webhook and return redirect** both go through the existing `runFulfilment`, which now has an offer branch:
   - The card amount is credited to the wallet once (unique session id) and one caller claims the session.
   - `fulfilOffer` then does everything in one transaction: the status change to PAID, the wallet debit, the PAID itemised multi-line invoice, the inactive custom Plan/GamePlan rows, the Server and the PROVISION job.
   - Server billing fields: `termMonths`, `termPromoPercent` (the discount), `grandfatheredRenewalCents` = renewal price, `annualDiscountPct = 0`, `refundableTermCents`, `expiresAt`, `autoRenew`, `wantsDedicatedIp`, and the pinned `nodeId`.
   - The card is saved for renewals.
6. **Races:**
   - A concurrent second caller changes nothing.
   - A failure after the card cleared (expired, withdrawn mid-checkout, wallet spent elsewhere, amount mismatch) leaves the money as wallet credit. The customer is notified and a staff task is opened.
   - A second payment for an already-paid offer stays as wallet credit with a "refund if they want it" task.
   - Cancelling an offer also expires its open checkout.
   - An offer accepted before expiry is still honoured for 2 hours after it expires.

Renewals match exactly: tests run the real `renewalCharge` function, and the created server renews at exactly the renewal price × term. Terms are monthly or annual only, because 24/36-month terms carry fixed platform discounts that would apply on top.

### Automated vs manual
**Automated:**
- Pricing, the frozen terms and expiry.
- The chat card and email.
- Wallet/card payment and the saved card.
- The invoice, Plan/Server rows and PROVISION job.
- Renewals through the normal billing sweep.
- Dedicated IP: assigned by the normal provision path, billed at the platform rate.

**Manual** (a task shows on `/admin/offers` until someone clicks "Mark done"):
- **CPU pinning:** `qm set --affinity`.
- **CPU priority:** `qm set --cpuunits`.
- **Dedicated servers:** the offer takes payment and writes the invoice, nothing is provisioned, and renewals must be invoiced by hand.

**Game offers:**
- They deploy with the game's order defaults.
- Required passwords are auto-generated, and the customer can change them in Settings.
- Not offerable, and hidden from the composer, because they need a value only the customer can give: fivem, dragonwilds, sunkenland, dst.

### Tests and evidence
- **Typecheck:** `npx tsc --noEmit` is clean.
- **Pure tests:** `test/offers-pricing.test.ts`, 17 tests.
- **Database tests:** `test/offers-db.test.ts`, 13 tests, opt-in via `OFFERS_TEST_DATABASE_URL` against a throwaway Postgres. They cover concurrent wallet accepts, the webhook + return race, duplicate payment, expiry/grace, withdraw mid-checkout, tampered terms, amount mismatch, dedicated, game, annual, chat-card shape and the pinned node. All 30 pass.
- **Full suite** (3,323 tests, 47 failures), compared by name against the 46-failure baseline:
  - All 46 baseline failures are among them and no baseline name went missing.
  - The one extra is `every active plan in the DB is in the bot's catalogue`. It fails only because I ran the suite against my throwaway DB, which has no real catalog. It is skipped when `DATABASE_URL` is unset, as in the baseline, and passes that way.
- **Stripe test mode:** real embedded checkout paid with card 4242. The offer went to PAID, one server and one PROVISION job were created with the correct fields, the ledger shows +3790/−3790, one PAID invoice, a CPU_PINNING and a CPU_PRIORITY task, and the card (visa 4242) was saved. Replaying the return URL twice created no duplicates.
- **Screenshots** in `/root/agent-notes/offers/`: composer (desktop and mobile), admin page after send, customer chat card (desktop and mobile), offer page (desktop and mobile), Stripe embedded checkout, after payment.
- **Docs:** a new section is appended to `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md`.
- **Not run:** a full `next build`, to keep CPU off node-1. The dev server compiled every new route and server action.
- **Cleanup:** dev server and throwaway Postgres are stopped. Scratch files are in `/tank/claude-scratch/offers-e2e` and `offers-pg`.

### Deploy steps
1. Merge the branch.
2. `npx prisma db push`: adds 3 tables and 2 enums, touches nothing else.
3. `npx prisma generate`.
4. Go through `deploy-staging.sh` → verify → `promote-production.sh`.

No new env vars or webhook events are needed.

### Risks and notes
- **Conflict with the live-chat overhaul:** I made a 3-line change in `components/ChatWidget.tsx` so offer cards render instead of crashing the plan-card renderer. That agent may get a trivial conflict there. The admin chat desk doesn't render cards yet; that is their side.
- **SUPPORT-only staff can't send offers.** Billing access is required, so the composer shows a clear refusal for them.
- **Chat offers need a signed-in visitor.** An anonymous thread is refused.
- **Pinned nodes skip the global RAM check.** The node's disk pool is still checked.
- **Dedicated IP renewals use the live price.** The first invoice uses the rate snapshotted at send, but renewals use whatever the dedicated-IP price setting is at that time.
- **Dedicated-server renewals are manual.**
- **`/admin/offers` has no pagination** (shows 200 offers, 100 tasks).
- **Auto-promoter:** this is a money path, so it shouldn't reach prod unreviewed. Per the existing note about an unidentified auto-promoter, don't push or merge it until it has been reviewed.
